title: Renal replacement therapy
summary: Renal replacement therapy in the ICU: when to start (AEIOU, STARRT-AKI, AKIKI 2), choosing CRRT, IHD or SLED, writing a CRRT prescription, citrate vs heparin, troubleshooting circuits, and antibiotic dosing on CRRT.

topics.title: Indications and timing of RRT
topics.summary: Absolute indications (AEIOU), why routine early RRT does not help (STARRT-AKI, AKIKI), and when not to delay further (AKIKI-2).

definition.text: Start RRT emergently for life-threatening complications of AKI not responding to medical therapy. Without these, a watchful-waiting strategy with close monitoring is safe; many patients recover without RRT.

steps.title: Check emergency indications (AEIOU)
steps.detail: A: acidosis pH < 7.15 (metabolic) refractory; E: K > 6.0-6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes refractory to medical therapy; I: intoxication with dialysable toxin (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylate, metformin with lactic acidosis, valproate); O: fluid overload with pulmonary oedema refractory to diuretics; U: uraemic complications (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).

steps.title: If none: watch and wait
steps.detail: Daily (or 12-hourly) review: urine output, fluid balance, K, bicarbonate, urea, creatinine. Optimise haemodynamics, stop nephrotoxins, try diuretics for overload.

steps.title: Do not delay beyond reasonable thresholds
steps.detail: AKIKI-2: when oliguria > 72 h or blood urea nitrogen > 112 mg/dL (urea ~240 mg/dL), postponing RRT further gave no benefit and possible harm.

steps.title: Consider the whole patient
steps.detail: Severe fluid overload (> 10% body weight) with worsening oxygenation, rising K with ongoing tissue breakdown (rhabdo, tumour lysis), or severe sepsis needing large volumes may justify earlier start.

steps.title: Discuss goals
steps.detail: In patients with poor prognosis, discuss whether RRT matches their goals of care before starting.

steps.title: Assess for recovery daily
steps.detail: Rising urine output (> 400-500 mL/day without diuretics, or > 2 L/day with diuretics) suggests recovery; trial off CRRT.

tables.title: Emergency indications for RRT
rows: K > 6.0-6.5 mmol/L or ECG changes; severe hyper/hyponatraemia with AKI; tumour lysis

redFlags.text: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes in anuric AKI: give calcium, insulin-dextrose and salbutamol as a bridge, and call for dialysis access now.

pitfalls.text: Starting RRT purely on a creatinine number in a stable, non-oliguric patient: exposes them to catheter and circuit risks with no benefit (STARRT-AKI more RRT dependence at 90 days).
Waiting indefinitely: in AKIKI-2, deferring beyond the thresholds was harmful.

pearls.text: In India blood urea (not BUN) is usually reported: BUN (mg/dL) ≈ urea (mg/dL) ÷ 2.14.

nodes.text: RRT consistent with goals of care?
Watchful waiting: 12-24 h review of UO, K, pH, fluids, urea
Oliguria > 72 h or BUN > 112 mg/dL, or worsening overload?

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: RRT replaces solute clearance and fluid removal but adds risks: catheter infection and thrombosis, hypotension, hypophosphataemia, drug and nutrient removal, and possibly delayed renal recovery from haemodynamic insults.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- AKIKI (2016): delayed strategy avoided RRT in 49% with similar mortality [Gaudry 2016].
- ELAIN (2016, single-centre surgical): early RRT reduced 90-day mortality; not replicated [Zarbock 2016].
- STARRT-AKI (2020, n=3,019): accelerated RRT did not reduce mortality and increased RRT dependence at 90 days [STARRT-AKI 2020].
- AKIKI 2 (2021): a more-delayed strategy beyond oliguria > 72 h or BUN > 112 mg/dL offered no benefit and was associated with harm [Gaudry 2021].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Which patients benefit from earlier RRT (e.g. severe overload, ARDS); biomarker-guided timing.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- Cost and availability of CRRT shape decisions in India; SLED on a standard dialysis machine is widely used.
- Dialysis for toxins: methanol outbreaks (illicit liquor) need urgent haemodialysis as fomepizole is scarce.

options: Did not reduce mortality and increased RRT dependence at 90 days

topics.title: CRRT vs IHD vs SLED
topics.summary: Choose the modality by haemodynamics, brain risk, resources and cost; understand convection vs diffusion and vascular access.

definition.text: IHD: 3-5 h sessions, fast clearance, more hypotension. CRRT (CVVH/CVVHD/CVVHDF): 24 h, gentle fluid removal, best for unstable patients and raised ICP. SLED/PIRRT: 6-12 h on a standard machine with low blood and dialysate flows: a cheaper hybrid.

steps.title: Choose by haemodynamics
steps.detail: Shock on vasopressors or needing large fluid removal: CRRT or SLED. Stable patients: IHD. KDIGO: use CRRT and IHD as complementary therapies.

steps.title: Brain at risk
steps.detail: Acute liver failure, TBI, cerebral oedema: CRRT preferred (avoids osmotic shifts and hypotension).

steps.title: Choose the technique
steps.detail: Convection (CVVH: replacement fluid; better middle-molecule removal) vs diffusion (CVVHD: dialysate) vs both (CVVHDF). Outcome differences are not proven; follow unit practice.

steps.title: Vascular access
steps.detail: Non-cuffed dialysis catheter, ultrasound-guided. Preference: right internal jugular (12-15 cm) > femoral (19-24 cm) > left internal jugular (15-20 cm) > subclavian (avoid: stenosis risk for future fistula).

steps.title: Prescribe fluid removal
steps.detail: Net ultrafiltration usually 0-2 mL/kg/h, adjusted hourly to haemodynamics; very high net UF (> 1.75 mL/kg/h) associated with worse outcomes in observational data.

steps.title: Monitor
steps.detail: Electrolytes (K, PO4, Mg) 6-12 hourly on CRRT, ABG, temperature (CRRT cools), drug levels, circuit pressures.

redFlags.text: Hypotension at the start of IHD/SLED: reduce UF, lower blood flow initially, cool dialysate, increase vasopressor; switch to CRRT if recurrent.

pitfalls.text: Subclavian dialysis catheters: high central vein stenosis risk that ruins future AV fistula access.
Forgetting that CRRT removes heat: hypothermia masks fever.

pearls.text: SLED on a standard haemodialysis machine using online dialysate is the cost-effective choice for unstable patients in many Indian ICUs.

nodes.text: Raised ICP / acute liver failure / cerebral oedema?
On vasopressors or needs large UF?
SLED / PIRRT 6-12 h on standard machine

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Diffusion moves small solutes (urea, K) down a concentration gradient; convection drags solutes with water through the membrane (solvent drag), clearing larger molecules. Slow continuous removal avoids rapid osmotic shifts (dialysis disequilibrium, cerebral oedema) and hypotension.
consultantNotes.evidence: - RCTs and meta-analyses show no mortality difference between CRRT and IHD; CRRT may be associated with better renal recovery in observational data [KDIGO 2012].
consultantNotes.controversies: - CVVH vs CVVHDF; high cut-off membranes; adsorptive filters (oXiris, CytoSorb) in sepsis - unproven.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- CRRT costs (filters, bags) run to tens of thousands of rupees per day; SLED with online fluid reduces cost several-fold.
- Many Indian ICUs depend on the hospital dialysis unit for IHD/SLED staffing; agree escalation pathways.

topics.title: Prescribing CRRT dose
topics.summary: Write a CRRT prescription: modality, blood flow, effluent dose 20-25 mL/kg/h delivered, fluids, net ultrafiltration, and monitoring.

definition.text: CRRT dose = effluent flow rate (replacement + dialysate + net UF) per kg per hour. KDIGO: deliver 20-25 mL/kg/h; prescribe ~25-30 mL/kg/h to allow for downtime. Higher doses (35-40) do not improve survival (RENAL, ATN).

steps.title: Modality and filter
steps.detail: CVVHDF (or CVVH) with a high-flux filter (~1.0-1.5 m²).

steps.title: Blood flow
steps.detail: Start 100-150 mL/min, increase to 150-250 mL/min as tolerated.

steps.title: Effluent dose
steps.detail: Prescribe 25-30 mL/kg/h (actual body weight). Example split CVVHDF: replacement and dialysate equally; pre-dilution replacement (part) prolongs filter life but reduces efficiency.

steps.title: Fluids
steps.detail: Bicarbonate-buffered solutions; adjust K (usually 4 mmol/L) and phosphate; avoid lactate buffer in liver failure/lactic acidosis.

steps.title: Net ultrafiltration
steps.detail: Set hourly target (e.g. 0-150 mL/h) based on fluid goals and haemodynamics; review every 4-6 h.

steps.title: Keep filtration fraction < 20-25%
steps.detail: FF = UF rate / plasma flow. High FF (convective, high UF, low blood flow, high haematocrit) clots filters. Use pre-dilution or increase blood flow.

steps.title: Monitor delivered dose
steps.detail: Record downtime (filter changes, procedures, CT); adjust prescription if delivered < 20 mL/kg/h.

tables.title: Worked CRRT prescription (70 kg, CVVHDF)
rows: Regional citrate (if no contraindication) or UFH
tables.caption: Example only; adjust to machine and unit protocol.

redFlags.text: Severe hypophosphataemia (< 1 mg/dL) and hypokalaemia are common after 24-48 h of CRRT: replace or use phosphate-containing solutions.

pitfalls.text: Prescribing exactly 20 mL/kg/h: downtime means delivered dose falls below target.
Ignoring the fluid balance of all other infusions (drugs, feeds) when setting net UF.

pearls.text: Higher effluent doses also remove more antibiotics, amino acids and trace elements; there is no benefit beyond 25 mL/kg/h.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Small-solute clearance on CRRT approximates effluent flow (fully saturated with urea in post-dilution or diffusion at low flows). Pre-dilution reduces solute concentration entering the filter, reducing clearance by ~15-20%.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- RENAL (1,508 patients): 40 vs 25 mL/kg/h effluent - no difference in 90-day mortality [RENAL 2009].
- ATN (1,124 patients): intensive vs less-intensive RRT - no difference in 60-day mortality [ATN 2008].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Dosing by actual vs ideal body weight in obesity; dose adaptation for sepsis or high catabolism.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Commercial CRRT fluids are expensive; some Indian units use locally prepared fluids with strict pharmacy protocols - infection and composition errors are risks.

quiz.explanation: RENAL and ATN trials support 20-25 mL/kg/h delivered.

quiz.stem: Filtration fraction should be kept below:
quiz.explanation: High FF causes haemoconcentration and filter clotting.
Delivered dose is usually lower than prescribed.

topics.title: Heparin vs citrate anticoagulation
topics.summary: Regional citrate as first choice for CRRT, heparin when citrate is unsuitable, and options in bleeding or HIT.

definition.text: KDIGO suggests regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) rather than heparin for CRRT in patients without contraindications, and heparin (UFH or LMWH) when citrate cannot be used. RICH (2020): citrate prolonged filter life with fewer bleeding complications.

steps.title: Assess bleeding and liver function
steps.detail: Active bleeding, recent surgery, platelets < 50 x10^9/L, coagulopathy: avoid systemic heparin. Severe liver failure or lactate > 4 mmol/L with shock: caution with citrate (accumulation).

steps.title: Citrate (first choice)
steps.detail: Pre-filter citrate to post-filter iCa 0.25-0.35 mmol/L; calcium infusion to systemic iCa 1.0-1.2 mmol/L. Check iCa at 1 h and 6-hourly.

steps.title: Detect citrate accumulation
steps.detail: Total Ca/ionised Ca ratio > 2.5, rising anion gap acidosis, falling systemic iCa despite increasing Ca infusion: reduce citrate/blood flow, increase dialysate, or switch method.

steps.title: Heparin (if citrate unsuitable)
steps.detail: UFH pre-filter 5-10 units/kg/h, aPTT target 45-60 s (or per protocol); avoid in HIT.

steps.title: No anticoagulation
steps.detail: In high bleeding risk: pre-dilution, higher blood flow (200-250 mL/min), low FF, minimise interruptions; accept shorter filter life.

steps.title: HIT
steps.detail: Stop all heparin; use citrate or argatroban (or no anticoagulation).

doseCards.workedExample: 70 kg at 7 units/kg/h = 490 units/h = 4.9 mL/h of 100 units/mL

redFlags.text: Rising anion gap, falling iCa and total/iCa > 2.5 on citrate = citrate accumulation: act now (risk of severe hypocalcaemia and acidosis).

pitfalls.text: Measuring 'systemic' iCa from the post-filter port.
Running citrate in a patient with acute liver failure and lactate 8 mmol/L without close monitoring.

pearls.text: Citrate also supplies bicarbonate (metabolised to bicarbonate in liver/muscle): watch for metabolic alkalosis and reduce bicarbonate in fluids.

nodes.text: Citrate contraindicated (severe liver failure, lactate > 4 with shock)?
No anticoagulation: pre-dilution, high blood flow, low FF

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Citrate chelates ionised calcium in the circuit, blocking the coagulation cascade only in the filter. Most citrate-calcium complexes are removed in the effluent; the remainder is metabolised (liver, muscle) to bicarbonate. Accumulation occurs when metabolism fails.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- RICH (596 patients): citrate vs heparin - longer filter life (47 vs 26 h), fewer bleeding complications, no 90-day mortality difference; more new infections in citrate group [Zarbock 2020].
- KDIGO 2012 suggests citrate for CRRT in patients without contraindications [KDIGO 2012].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Citrate in liver failure: increasingly used with careful monitoring.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Citrate solutions are not available in many Indian ICUs; heparin or no-anticoagulation CRRT/SLED is common. Filter cost makes filter life an important outcome.

topics.title: Filter clotting and CRRT troubleshooting
topics.summary: Read circuit pressures, fix access problems, prevent early filter clotting and handle common alarms.

definition.text: Common CRRT problems: access (arterial) pressure too negative, high return pressure, rising transmembrane pressure (TMP) and pressure drop = filter clotting, air alarms, blood leak.

steps.title: Read the pressures
steps.detail: Access pressure (normally -50 to -150 mmHg), return pressure (+50 to +150), filter pressure, effluent pressure, TMP (rising > 200-250 mmHg suggests clotting), pressure drop across filter (rising = clotting).

steps.title: Access alarms (very negative pressure)
steps.detail: Catheter kinked, patient position (femoral - straighten leg), catheter against vessel wall, thrombus. Reposition, flush with saline, reverse lines (increases recirculation), reduce blood flow; replace catheter if persistent.

steps.title: High return pressure
steps.detail: Kink or clot in return limb/venous chamber, catheter problem. Check line, chamber, catheter.

steps.title: Early filter clotting (< 24 h)
steps.detail: Check anticoagulation (citrate post-filter iCa, aPTT), catheter function, FF > 25%, frequent interruptions, high haematocrit. Increase blood flow, increase pre-dilution, reduce net UF, optimise catheter (right IJ, correct length).

steps.title: Return blood before the filter clots fully
steps.detail: If TMP rising rapidly, return blood to the patient (saves ~150-200 mL blood) and replace the circuit.

steps.title: Patient-side issues
steps.detail: Hypothermia (use warmer), hypotension at connection (prime with saline/albumin, start low blood flow), electrolyte drift (6-12 hourly labs), catheter infection.

redFlags.text: Repeated circuit loss means repeated blood loss (~150-200 mL each) and underdosed therapy: fix the cause, not just the filter.

pitfalls.text: Reversing lines as routine: increases recirculation and lowers clearance.

pearls.text: Femoral catheters must reach the IVC (19-24 cm) to reduce recirculation and access problems.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Filter clotting results from blood-membrane contact activation, haemoconcentration at the filter outlet (especially with high post-dilution UF), blood stasis during flow interruptions, and inadequate anticoagulation.
consultantNotes.evidence: - KDIGO and RICH data: citrate and adequate catheter function are the main determinants of filter life [KDIGO 2012; RICH 2020].
consultantNotes.controversies: - Routine filter change interval (often 72 h maximum per manufacturer).
consultantNotes.indiaNotes: - Filters are the major cost item; filter lives under 24 h are common without citrate. Audit filter life monthly.

topics.title: Antibiotic dosing on CRRT and SLED
topics.summary: Avoid underdosing: full loading doses, CRRT maintenance roughly equal to CrCl 25-50 mL/min, and timing doses around IHD/SLED.

definition.text: CRRT at 20-25 mL/kg/h clears drugs roughly like a native CrCl of ~25-50 mL/min. Underdosing beta-lactams is common and dangerous in sepsis. IHD and SLED remove large amounts during sessions: give doses after the session.

steps.title: Give full loading doses
steps.detail: Always the normal loading dose regardless of RRT.

steps.title: Maintenance on CRRT
steps.detail: Dose for CrCl ~25-50 mL/min equivalent for renally cleared drugs; higher for very high effluent rates. Prefer extended/continuous infusion for beta-lactams.

steps.title: IHD / SLED timing
steps.detail: Give doses after dialysis or SLED sessions (or supplement after). SLED clears drugs substantially - doses resemble CRRT or higher.

steps.title: Therapeutic drug monitoring
steps.detail: Vancomycin and aminoglycosides by levels; beta-lactam TDM where available.

steps.title: Adjust when RRT stops or kidneys recover
steps.detail: Re-dose to native function; avoid accumulation when CRRT is interrupted for long periods.

consultantNotes.pathophysiology: Drug removal by CRRT depends on molecular size, protein binding (only free drug is filtered), volume of distribution and effluent rate. Highly protein-bound or large-Vd drugs (e.g. ceftriaxone, linezolid, polymyxin B) are minimally affected.
consultantNotes.evidence:
- Hoff 2020 review summarises dosing for IHD, PIRRT and CRRT for common antibiotics [Hoff 2020].
- Pharmacokinetic studies show frequent beta-lactam underexposure on CRRT with traditional renal doses.
consultantNotes.controversies: - Optimal beta-lactam targets (100% fT > MIC vs 4x MIC); availability of TDM.
consultantNotes.indiaNotes:
- CRE and colistin/polymyxin use are common in Indian ICUs; polymyxin B is often preferred in AKI/RRT because it needs no renal adjustment.
- Involve a clinical pharmacist where available; publish a unit-level CRRT dosing chart.

drugs.name: Trisodium citrate (regional citrate anticoagulation)
drugs.indications: First-line CRRT anticoagulation (KDIGO) in patients without contraindication
drugs.adultDose: Pre-filter citrate (e.g. 4% trisodium citrate or citrate-containing replacement fluid) dosed to achieve post-filter ionised Ca 0.25-0.35 mmol/L; systemic calcium chloride/gluconate infusion post-filter to keep patient ionised Ca 1.0-1.2 mmol/L.
drugs.preparationIndia: Commercial citrate solutions (e.g. 4% trisodium citrate, Prismocitrate/Regiocit) - availability limited in India; machine-specific protocols.
drugs.cautions: Citrate accumulation in liver failure, severe lactic acidosis (lactate > 4 mmol/L) or severe shock: high anion gap acidosis, total/ionised Ca ratio > 2.5. Metabolic alkalosis and hypernatraemia with excessive citrate.
drugs.monitoring: Post-filter and systemic iCa at 1 h, then 6-hourly; total Ca daily; ABG, Na, Mg.
drugs.verify: Protocol is machine- and solution-specific; follow the manufacturer's/unit protocol.

drugs.name: Unfractionated heparin (CRRT circuit)
drugs.indications: CRRT circuit anticoagulation when citrate is unavailable or contraindicated
drugs.adultDose: Optional priming; pre-filter infusion 5-10 units/kg/h (typically 300-1,000 units/h), titrated to aPTT 45-60 s (≈ 1.5x control) or per local protocol.
drugs.preparationIndia: 25,000 units in 50 mL NS = 500 units/mL (or 5,000 units in 50 mL = 100 units/mL for low-dose circuit use).
drugs.cautions: Bleeding, HIT (switch to citrate/argatroban). Avoid if active bleeding or platelets < 50 x10^9/L.
drugs.verify: Target aPTT and dose vary widely between Indian units; align with local CRRT protocol.

drugs.name: Meropenem
drugs.adultDose: CRRT (effluent 20-25 mL/kg/h): 1 g q8h (2 g q8h for CNS or high MIC). IHD: 500 mg-1 g q24h, dose after dialysis. SLED: 1 g q12h (after session).
drugs.preparationIndia: 500 mg and 1 g vials; extended infusion over 3 h.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-tazobactam
drugs.adultDose: CRRT: 4.5 g q8h (or 3.375 g q6h); extended infusion. IHD: 2.25 g q8-12h + dose after dialysis.

drugs.name: Vancomycin
drugs.adultDose: Load 20-25 mg/kg (actual body weight) for all; CRRT maintenance ~15 mg/kg q24h (or 7.5-10 mg/kg q12h) guided by levels (trough 15-20 mg/L or AUC 400-600). IHD: 15-25 mg/kg load, then 500-1,000 mg after each session by pre-dialysis levels.
drugs.preparationIndia: 500 mg and 1 g vials; infuse ≤ 10 mg/min.

drugs.name: Colistin (colistimethate sodium)
drugs.adultDose: Load 300 mg colistin base activity (CBA) = 9 million units. CRRT: maintenance ~220-440 mg CBA/day in divided doses (international consensus suggests higher doses due to clearance). IHD: daily dose on non-dialysis days + supplemental dose after dialysis.
drugs.preparationIndia: 1 million and 2 million unit vials (1 million units ≈ 33 mg CBA).
drugs.cautions: Nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity; dose labelling confusion (units vs mg CBA vs mg CMS).
drugs.verify: Colistin dosing on CRRT is uncertain; follow the 2019 international polymyxin consensus or ICU pharmacist.
